concepts.name: Pointers from both ends of a sorted array (Two Sum II)
Container With Most Water: move the shorter line

questions.prompt: Two Sum II: `numbers` is sorted. With `left` at the start and `right` at the end, `numbers[left] + numbers[right]` is less than `target`. What do you do, and why?

choices.text: Move `right` left, because the sum needs to get smaller
Move both pointers inward, because neither element can be used
Restart from `left + 1` and scan every `right` position again
Move `left` right: `numbers[left]` is too small even with the largest value

questions.explanation: `numbers[right]` is the largest value still in range, so if even it isn't enough, `numbers[left]` can't be in any answer with the remaining elements and can be dropped. Symmetrically, a sum above the target drops `right`. Each step discards one element for good, so the search is O(n) time with O(1) extra space, as the problem requires.

sources.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
sources.claim: numbers is 1-indexed and sorted in non-decreasing order, exactly one solution exists, and the solution must use only constant extra space.

questions.prompt: What does Two Sum II return for `numbers = [2, 7, 11, 15]`, `target = 9`?

choices.text: `[0, 1]`, the zero-based indices of 2 and 7
`[1, 2]`, because the problem uses 1-indexed positions
`[1, 4]`, the first and last positions
`[2, 7]`, the two values that add up to 9

questions.explanation: 2 + 15 = 17 is too big, so `right` moves to 11; 2 + 11 = 13 is still too big; 2 + 7 = 9 matches. The problem says the array is 1-indexed and asks for `[index1, index2]`, so you return `[left + 1, right + 1]`, which is `[1, 2]`. Returning zero-based indices is a common slip.

sources.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
sources.claim: For numbers = [2,7,11,15] and target = 9 the output is [1,2], since the problem returns 1-indexed positions.

questions.prompt: Explain why the two-pointer approach to Two Sum II never misses the answer, and why it needs the array to be sorted.

model_answer.summary: Because the array is sorted, a sum that is too small proves the left element can't pair with anything still in range, and a sum that is too big proves the same for the right element, so each move discards only elements that can't be in the answer.
key_points: Sorted order means `numbers[left]` is the smallest remaining value and `numbers[right]` the largest
If the sum is below the target, `numbers[left]` plus any remaining value is at most that sum, so `left` can't be in the answer and moves right
If the sum is above the target, `numbers[right]` is too big with any remaining value, so `right` moves left
Each step removes one element that can't be in a solution, so the answer is never skipped and there are at most n − 1 steps: O(n) time, O(1) space
Without sorting, the sum says nothing about which pointer to move, so the argument fails

questions.explanation: Two pointers is a proof by elimination: every move must be justified by showing that the discarded element can't be part of the answer. Sorted order is what makes that justification possible.

sources.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
sources.claim: The input array is sorted in non-decreasing order, has exactly one solution, and must be solved with constant extra space.

questions.prompt: Valid Palindrome ignores case and all non-alphanumeric characters. What should it return for `"0P"`?

choices.text: `false`: lowercased it's `"0p"`, and `'0'` isn't `'p'`
`true`: digits are ignored, which leaves only `"p"`
`true`: every string of length 2 or less is a palindrome
`false`: the input contains a character that isn't a letter

questions.explanation: The problem keeps letters and numbers, so `'0'` stays and is compared with `'p'`. A common bug filters with `str.isalpha()`, which drops digits and wrongly returns `true` here; use `str.isalnum()`. With two pointers you skip non-alphanumeric characters from each end and compare lowercased characters, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

sources.title: Valid Palindrome
sources.claim: A phrase is a palindrome after lowercasing and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, where alphanumeric characters include letters and numbers.

sources.title: Built-in Types — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: str.isalnum() is true for characters that are alphabetic or numeric, whereas str.isalpha() is true only for Unicode letters.

questions.prompt: In the two-pointer Valid Palindrome, when does the loop stop and return `true`?

choices.text: When `left` reaches the end of the string
When the first pair of characters match
When `left` and `right` meet or cross with no mismatch
When every character has been compared twice

questions.explanation: The pointers move toward each other, skipping characters that aren't letters or digits, and compare lowercased characters; any mismatch returns `false` at once. Once `left >= right`, every pair has been checked, so the string is a palindrome. A string with no alphanumeric characters, such as `" "`, is empty after filtering and counts as a palindrome.

sources.title: Valid Palindrome
sources.claim: For s = " " the answer is true: after removing non-alphanumeric characters the empty string reads the same both ways.

questions.prompt: 3Sum sorts `nums`, then for each index `i` runs two pointers over the rest. Why does it skip `i` when `i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]`?

choices.text: Because a repeated value can never be part of a triplet
Because the two-pointer search only works on distinct values
To make the algorithm O(n log n) instead of O(n²)
That value already had its turn as `nums[i]`, so its triplets would repeat

questions.explanation: The answer must not contain duplicate triplets. After sorting, equal values sit together, and the first of them has already found every triplet starting with that value, so the repeats are skipped. Repeated values can still appear within a triplet: `[-1, -1, 2]` is valid. The skip saves work, but the algorithm stays O(n²).

sources.title: 3Sum
sources.claim: 3Sum returns all triplets summing to zero with distinct indices, and the solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.

questions.prompt: 3Sum on `[-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]`, sorted to `[-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]`. What should it return, and what goes wrong without any duplicate skipping?

choices.text: `[[-1, 0, 1]]`; without skipping it also returns `[-1, -1, 2]`
`[[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]`; without skipping, `[-1, 0, 1]` appears twice
`[[-1, 0, 1], [0, 1, -1]]`; skipping removes the reordered copy

questions.explanation: With `i` at the first -1, the pointers find `[-1, -1, 2]` and `[-1, 0, 1]`. With `i` at the second -1, they find `[-1, 0, 1]` again, which skipping an `i` equal to the previous one prevents. There is only one 2, so `[-4, 2, 2]` isn't possible.

sources.title: 3Sum
sources.claim: For nums = [-1,0,1,2,-1,-4] the expected output is [[-1,-1,2],[-1,0,1]].

questions.prompt: Describe the duplicate-skipping logic in 3Sum, and explain why each part is needed.

model_answer.summary: Sort first; skip an `i` whose value equals the previous one; after recording a triplet, move `left` past values equal to the one just used, so the same triplet isn't recorded twice.
key_points: Sort the array first so equal values are next to each other
In the outer loop, skip `i` when `i > 0` and `nums[i] == nums[i - 1]`, because that value has already been tried as the first element
After recording a triplet, move `left` forward past values equal to the one just used, e.g. `while left < right and nums[left] == nums[left - 1]: left += 1`
Without the inner skip, an input like `[-2, 0, 0, 2, 2]` records `[-2, 0, 2]` twice
The whole algorithm is O(n²): O(n log n) to sort plus an O(n) two-pointer pass for each `i`

questions.explanation: Both skips rely on sorting: once equal values are adjacent, a repeat is always the same as its neighbour. The outer skip avoids repeating a first element, and the inner skip avoids repeating the second (the third then follows, since the sum is fixed).

sources.title: 3Sum
sources.claim: The answer must contain every zero-sum triplet with distinct indices but no duplicate triplets.

sources.title: Built-in Functions — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: sorted() returns a new sorted list, which places equal values next to each other.

questions.prompt: Container With Most Water: the left line has height 1, the right line height 7, and they are 8 apart. Which pointer do you move, and why?

choices.text: The left one: any other container with that line is narrower and at most 1 high
The right one: the taller line has already given the best area it can
Both: the area depends only on the width, which shrinks the same either way
Either one: the next area is the same whichever of the two pointers moves

questions.explanation: The area is `min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left)`. Every other container using the shorter line is narrower and still capped at height 1, so none can beat the current 1 × 8 = 8, and that line can be dropped. Moving the taller line instead keeps the cap of 1 (or lowers it) while the width shrinks, so it can't help.

sources.title: Container With Most Water
sources.claim: Two lines and the x-axis form a container whose water is bounded by the shorter line times the distance between them; return the maximum.

questions.prompt: What is the answer to Container With Most Water for `height = [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]`?

choices.text: 64, from the two 8s times the full width of 8
40, from the two lines of height 8 at indices 1 and 6
49, from heights 8 and 7 at indices 1 and 8
8, from the first and last lines at full width

questions.explanation: Starting at both ends: min(1, 7) × 8 = 8, so move the shorter left line. Then min(8, 7) × 7 = 49, and no later pair beats it. The two 8s give only 8 × 5 = 40, because width counts as much as height, and they aren't at the ends, so 64 isn't possible.

sources.title: Container With Most Water
sources.claim: For height = [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7] the maximum area is 49.

questions.prompt: In Container With Most Water, explain why moving the pointer at the shorter line is safe, and why the algorithm is O(n).

model_answer.summary: Every container that keeps the shorter line is narrower and no taller than the current one, so that line can be discarded; each step discards one line, so there are at most n − 1 steps.
key_points: The area is the shorter of the two heights times the distance between the lines
Every other container using the shorter line is narrower and still limited by that line's height, so none holds more than the current one
So the shorter line can safely be dropped, which is what moving its pointer does
Moving the taller line can't help: the width shrinks and the height is still capped by the shorter line
Each step drops one line, so the loop runs at most n − 1 times: O(n) time and O(1) space

questions.explanation: This is the same elimination argument as in Two Sum II: each move is justified by showing that no container using the discarded line could be the answer. Being able to state that argument is what interviewers listen for.

sources.title: Container With Most Water
sources.claim: The container is formed by two lines and the x-axis and cannot be slanted, so its capacity is the shorter height times the width; 2 <= n <= 10^5.
